lead: A vehicle speed loop compares reference and measured speed and commands tractive force. A PI controller removes steady-state speed error; a PD controller adds damping. The vehicle is modelled as a first-order lag, so two gains and one time constant describe the loop. Cruise control, electric-vehicle torque control and ADAS speed tracking use this. Only a few universities teach the tuning method here.
prereq: You need: Chapter 5.2 for the cruise loop, and first-order lag plus Laplace transforms from a control course.

sections.h3: Plant, PI law and lambda tuning

blocks.where: m is mass (kg); v is speed (m/s); F is tractive force (N); b is resistance (N per m/s).

blocks.text: Rearranged, τ dv/dt + v = K F, with τ = m/b in s and K = 1/b in (m/s)/N. In Laplace form, V(s)/F(s) = K/(τs + 1).

Error e = v_ref − v, with v_ref the wanted speed. PI law: u = Kp e + Ki ∫e dt, where u is commanded force (N), Kp is N per (m/s), and Ki is N/m (newton per metre of integrated speed error; Ki = Kp/Ti). Proportional action alone leaves an offset. At steady state Kp(v_ref − v) = b v, so e_ss = b v_ref/(Kp + b). For Kp much larger than b this is close to b v_ref/Kp. The integral supplies the force and drives e to zero.

Lambda tuning chooses closed-loop time constant λ: Kp = τ/(K λ), Ti = τ, Ki = Kp/Ti. Smaller λ gives faster response but larger force, so check actuator saturation. A reference model filters v_ref, often as 1/(λs + 1), before the loop sees it. On a real vehicle with a rate-limited actuator this slows the demanded force and limits saturation and overshoot; in the ideal first-order loop modelled here the loop already has no overshoot, so the main gain is a smooth force command.

PD law u = Kp e + Kd de/dt, where Kd is N per (m/s²). The derivative predicts error growth and opposes fast speed change, adding damping. With constant v_ref, de/dt = −dv/dt, so derivative on measurement is u = Kp e − Kd dv/dt. This avoids a kick when v_ref steps.

Measured speed carries sensor noise. A raw derivative amplifies it, so filter the derivative with time constant Tf, or use a small Kd. The derivative path becomes s/(Tf s + 1): a first-order lag with time constant Tf (in s) on the derivative. PI plus reference model is common for speed; PD alone cannot remove offset because at steady state de/dt = 0. Full Bode and root-locus design belongs to a control course.

For a step v_ref, the reference filter slows the demanded force before the PI block. The loop sees a gentle ramp, not a jump. On real vehicles this limits actuator saturation and overshoot; with the ideal lambda-tuned loop the response is already first order, so the main benefit is a smooth force command, not lower overshoot.

figure.caption: The loop holds 30 m/s: PI turns error into tractive force, the 1500 kg vehicle responds, and measured speed feeds back.

spec.title: PI speed loop for a 1500 kg vehicle
spec.aria: A reference speed of 30 m/s minus the measured speed forms the error; the PI block turns it into tractive force, the vehicle responds, and the measured speed closes the loop.

examples.question: A 1500 kg vehicle has resistance b = 100 N per m/s. (a) Find K and τ. (b) Choose λ = 3 s and find Kp, Ti, Ki. (c) With v_ref = 30 m/s, find the steady error if only proportional action is used.
steps: At steady state with proportional-only control, 500(30 − v) = 100v, so v = 25 m/s and e = 30 − 25 = 5 m/s. The shortcut b v_ref/Kp = 3000/500 = 6 m/s is only an upper bound, good when Kp is much larger than b. The integral term supplies the needed force and e falls to zero.
examples.answer: K = 0.01 (m/s)/N, τ = 15 s, Kp = 500 N/(m/s), Ki = 33.3 N/m, and proportional-only offset = 5 m/s (exact; the shortcut 3000/500 = 6 m/s is an upper bound).
examples.check:
m = 1500.0
b = 100.0
K = 1.0 / b
tau = m / b
lam = 3.0
Kp = tau / (K * lam)
Ti = tau
Ki = Kp / Ti
v_ref = 30.0
v_ss = Kp * v_ref / (Kp + b)
e_ss = v_ref - v_ss
print(f'{K:.2f}')
print(f'{tau:.0f}')
print(f'{Kp:.0f}')
print(f'{Ki:.1f}')
print(f'{e_ss:.0f}')
print(f'{v_ss:.0f}')

traps: Error sign: e = v_ref − v, not v − v_ref.
Kp alone leaves a steady offset; the integral term removes it.
Derivative on noisy measured speed amplifies noise; filter it.
Units: Kp N per m/s; Ki N/m; Kd N per (m/s²).
Too small λ demands huge force and saturates the actuator.

quiz.q: State the PI speed law and define Kp, Ki and e.
quiz.a: u = Kp e + Ki ∫e dt; e = v_ref − v; Kp is N per (m/s); Ki is N/m (Ki = Kp/Ti).

quiz.q: Why does integral action remove steady-state speed error?
quiz.a: At steady state the integral holds whatever force is needed, so the error can fall to zero; proportional action alone would need a nonzero error.

quiz.q: For m = 1200 kg, b = 120 N per m/s and λ = 4 s, find K, τ, Kp, Ti and Ki.
A PD loop uses raw measured speed and the signal is noisy. What happens, and what is the fix?
quiz.a: The derivative amplifies noise and the force chatters. Filter the derivative or use derivative on measurement with small Kd.

quiz.q: Kp = 400 N per (m/s); resistance at the set speed is 2400 N. Estimate the proportional-only speed error, then give the exact expression.
quiz.a: Estimate e ≈ 2400/400 = 6 m/s. Exact e = 2400/(400 + b) < 6 m/s, where b is the resistance coefficient in N per (m/s).

quiz.q: What does a reference model do before the PI loop?
quiz.a: It filters v_ref, often as 1/(λs + 1), so the loop sees a smooth setpoint instead of a step. On real vehicles this limits actuator saturation and gives a smooth force command; in the ideal first-order loop modelled here it does not lower overshoot.

beyond: Not for the exam. In production, speed loops run in software at a fixed sample rate, with anti-windup and feedforward from road grade. EV torque control schedules gains because mass and τ change with load. Reference models appear in adaptive cruise and robot velocity control. Search: lambda tuning, derivative on measurement, anti-windup, feedforward speed control.
